arXiv:2509.21979v1 [cs.CV] 26 Sep 2025

Benchmarking and Mitigate Psychological Sycophancy in Medical Vision-Language Models

Zikun Guo Affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence    Xinyue Xu Affiliation: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology    Pei Xiang Affiliation: Xidian University    Shu Yang Affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology    Xin Han Affiliation: Zhejiang A&F University    Di Wang Affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology    Lijie Hu Affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Abstract

Vision language models(VLMs) are increasingly integrated into clinical workflows, but they often exhibit sycophantic behavior prioritizing alignment with user phrasing social cues or perceived authority over evidence based reasoning. This study evaluate clinical sycophancy in medical visual question answering through a novel clinically grounded benchmark. We propose a medical sycophancy dataset construct from PathVQA, SLAKE, and VQA-RAD stratified by different type organ system and modality. Using psychologically motivated pressure templates including various sycophancy. In our adversarial experiments on various VLMs, we found that these models are generally vulnerable, exhibiting significant variations in the occurrence of adversarial responses, with weak correlations to the model accuracy or size. Imitation and expert provided corrections were found to be the most effective triggers, suggesting that the models possess a bias mechanism independent of visual evidence. To address this, we propose Visual Information Purification for Evidence based Response (VIPER) a lightweight mitigation strategy that filters non evidentiary content for example social pressures and then generates constrained evidence first answers. This framework reduces sycophancy by an average amount outperforming baselines while maintaining interpretability. Our benchmark analysis and mitigation framework lay the groundwork for robust deployment of medical VLMs in real world clinician interactions emphasizing the need for evidence anchored defenses.

1 Introduction

Artificial intelligence has become integral to medical imaging and clinical decision support, with vision language models (VLMs) enabling instruction following interfaces over visual evidence [24, 18]. While aggregate accuracy on public benchmarks continues to improve [17, 13, 29], safe deployment in healthcare requires reliability under distributional and interactional shift. Such reliability includes calibrated confidence, principled abstention, controllability, and robustness to human factors arising in medical model dialogue [14]. Absent these properties, nominal performance can mask brittleness that degrades clinical utility in routine workflows.

This study examines sycophancy, defined as a systematic tendency of models to align with user phrasing, perceived authority, or social cues at the expense of task evidence. Operationally, sycophancy constitutes a social influence induced distribution shift that perturbs the decision boundary toward agreement rather than veracity. In clinical communication, prompts frequently embed deference signals, emotional framing, or claims of consensus, these inputs can redirect attention away from image grounded findings and conflict with evidence based practice. Consequently, sycophancy represents a mechanism level threat to behavioral reliability that is distinct from canonical covariate shift or adversarial noise.

Although sycophancy has been documented in large language models [20, 14], its prevalence, drivers, and impact in medical VLMs remain insufficiently characterized. Multimodality introduces additional failure modes: non evidentiary textual tokens can modulate how visual features are parsed and weighted, and instruction following objectives may amplify compliance with socially charged tokens. Existing medical VLM evaluations emphasize capability and utility but rarely isolate vulnerabilities arising from realistic social influence within clinical dialogue [18, 24]. This gap limits principled assessment of behavioral robustness and impedes targeted mitigation.

An evaluation protocol for clinical sycophancy should satisfy key desiderata. First, pressure stimuli must be ecologically valid with respect to medical model interactions (e.g., expert correction, consensus cues, emotional framing) [5, 4]. Second, susceptibility must be isolated from baseline performance by applying pressure only to items answered correctly at baseline, this avoids conflating valid correction of erroneous answers with sycophancy. Third, items should balance medical domains and question types to avoid confounding effects. Fourth, measurements should support comparability across diverse model classes. Finally, analyses should attribute effects to pressure types rather than incidental prompt artifacts. These criteria motivate a benchmark that targets mechanism rather than surface perturbations.

We present a unified framework that satisfies these requirements. We curate a clinically motivated challenge set from established medical visual question answering resources with expert screening, instantiate a taxonomy of psychologically grounded pressure templates that reflect common communication patterns in clinical workflows, and evaluate contemporary VLMs under paired no pressure and pressured conditions. Our design isolates sycophancy as the proportion of initially correct responses that flip under pressure, supports cross model comparisons, and enables principled analysis of pressure specific effects. Full protocol details, dataset construction, and statistical procedures appear in Methods.

Empirically, broad but varied vulnerability is observed across model classes. Mimicry emerges as the dominant trigger at the aggregate level, instruction tuned general purpose systems tend to exhibit greater resistance than narrowly specialized medical models, and high baseline accuracy does not guarantee stability under social influence. These findings suggest an interaction between alignment objectives and compliance pressure, underscoring the need for defenses that re anchor inference on image evidence rather than conversational cues.

This study introduces VIPER (Visual Information Purification for Evidence based Response), a mitigation tailored to the observed failure mechanism. Competing prompting baselines include role based prompting, standard chain of thought, and visually guided cues. VIPER adopts an internal two stage scheme that (1) filters non evidentiary content and re centers the internal representation on image grounded inputs, then (2) produces an answer in a constrained, evidence first format. This decoupling reduces exposure of generation to socially charged tokens while preserving access to visual features, improving resistance to sycophancy without additional tools.

This work makes three contributions. First, we provide a clinically motivated evaluation protocol and challenge set for quantifying sycophancy in medical VLMs under realistic social pressures. Second, we deliver a cross model analysis that characterizes susceptibility patterns and relates them to model scale. Third, we propose a simple, deployment friendly mitigation that reduces sycophancy while maintaining diagnostic reasoning and interpretability. Together, these elements establish a foundation for assessing and improving behavioral reliability in multimodal clinical AI and inform the design of future training, prompting, and governance strategies.

Figure 1 provides a compact end to end overview that mirrors the narrative of the Introduction. Panel (a) illustrates a canonical sycophancy setting in medical VQA: a model that answers a baseline multiple choice question correctly subsequently flips to a pressured alternative when exposed to realistic social cues (e.g., expert correction, emotional appeal). The example emphasizes that the failure arises from social influence rather than missing visual evidence. Panel (b) summarizes the construction of our challenge set: items are drawn from PathVQA[8], SLAKE[15] and VQA-RAD[12] with expert screening, balanced coverage across organs and question types, and paired evaluation of the initial (no pressure) and pressured responses. Panel (c) presents our mitigation, VIPER. The first stage filters non evidentiary content (content filter), explicitly discarding external pressure, criticism, and role prompts, the second stage answers strictly from image evidence in a constrained format (medical expert role). This internal phase separation rather than additional tools or multi agent debate anchors inference on visual features and reduces conformity driven flips.

This study quantifies susceptibility to clinically plausible social pressures across contemporary systems, examines type and dataset specific effects using a balanced challenge set, benchmarks mitigation strategies and introduces a lightweight content filter plus evidence first scheme (VIPER), and provides attention level analyses that explain why it is effective.

2 Results

We first quantify broad but varied sycophantic susceptibility and its weak coupling to baseline accuracy (Fig. 2). We then validate type and dataset specific effects with a balanced challenge set and a clinically grounded pressure taxonomy (Fig. 3). Building on these insights, we benchmark mitigation strategies and show that VIPER achieves the best resistance and restoration balance across types and systems (Fig. 4). Finally, attention level dynamics reveal why VIPER works, showing pressure induced shifts away from evidence and VIPER driven re centering (Fig. 5).

2.1 Dataset and splits

We evaluate on a curated challenge set of 5,000 medical VQA items constructed from PathVQA[8], SLAKE[15] and VQA-RAD[12] with stratified sampling across question types and datasets (Fig. 3a). Items are balanced to provide representative coverage of short form queries (e.g., yes/no, where) and content questions (what/how/abnormality/object), and to avoid confounding by answer frequency. For each model, Stage 1 establishes baseline answers without social pressure, and Stage 2 applies seven clinically plausible pressure types to initially correct answers to measure sycophancy (Methods §4.4). All figures report aggregate measurements, and Appendix tables provide per model values with 95% confidence intervals obtained by bootstrap.

2.2 Baseline validation under no pressure conditions

We first validate baseline performance on medical VQA without pressure. Across the evaluated model classes (commercial, medical specialized, and open source), initial accuracy varies substantially (Fig. 2c, left). Models trained with extensive instruction following objectives generally achieve stronger baseline accuracy, whereas some narrowly specialized medical models exhibit higher variance. These results establish that all types possess non trivial competence on the task, providing a stable reference point for subsequent susceptibility analyses. The paired no pressure and pressured protocol that anchors our analysis is depicted in panel (b) of Fig. 1.

Category level comparisons indicate that baseline performance alone does not predict interaction robustness. Even models with competitive accuracy show divergent behavior once conversational pressure is introduced (Fig. 2b). This motivates decoupling "can do the task" from "will maintain evidence grounded answers under pressure".

2.3 Systematic evaluation of sycophantic susceptibility

We assess sycophancy by applying the seven pressure types to items initially answered correctly and measuring the flip rate. Figure 2 consolidates the results across pressure potency, model series, and cross pressure structure.

Top line effects (Figure 2a). Mimicry is the most potent trigger across systems; Expert correction and technological self doubt form a consistent second tier; authority based and Ethical and Economic are generally moderate; Social consensus exhibits high cross model variance. Appendix Table 1 reports extrema (e.g., Claude-3-Haiku 96.61% under Expert; DentoBot 97.22% under Mimicry; LLaVA-13B 86.81% under Expert; Qwen2.5-VL-7B 96.87% under Mimicry). Macro averaged sycophancy spans 26.67%-80.26% across models.

Model wise variability (Figure 2c,d). Ordering by overall sycophancy places several commercial systems at the high end, medical specialized models in the middle with large dispersion, and open source Qwen2.5-VL [1] variants at the low end. The accuracy versus sycophancy scatter shows weak coupling, and marker area indicates that parameter scale is not monotonic with robustness. Differences align more closely with alignment regimen and instruction tuning than with scale or baseline accuracy. Notable outliers include comparatively robust Qwen2.5-VL-3B/32B [1], mid pack GPT-4o [10] with varied type sensitivity, elevated LLaVA-13B [16] relative to its series, and MedDR [7] with authority adjacent concentration.

Distributional structure and cross pressure dependencies (Figure 2f). Series level distributions reveal heavier upper tails for commercial and narrowly medical specialized series than for open source counterparts, indicating more frequent extreme flips; open source series display tighter interquartile ranges yet retain outliers for Mimicry and Expert. The correlation matrix exhibits coherent clusters: authority based with expert correction; emotional with social consensus; technological self doubt moderately with authority cues and partly distinct from Mimicry supporting a shared compliance factor with type specific expression. Quantitative correlations appear in Appendix Table 8; a tail risk summary by ecosystem using UR90 (90th percentile across pressure types) appears in Appendix Table 9.

Vulnerability signatures ((Figure 2e)). Model heatmaps show broad, intense bands for some models (for example, Doubao-Vision [22] and Claude-3 [9]), indicating generalized susceptibility, and lighter, structured bands for others (for example, Qwen2.5-VL-3B/32B), indicating comparatively uniform resistance. Mixed within row patterns imply that training objectives and prompt interfaces selectively shape how social cues are internalized.

Collectively, these results show that sycophancy is widespread yet structured: pressure potency is ranked and correlated, robustness is only weakly coupled to baseline accuracy or scale, and models exhibit stable, model specific signatures. These observations motivate the targeted mitigation analysis in Fig. 4; supplementary quantification of cross pressure correlations and series tails appears in the Appendix.

2.4 Mechanism and control analyses

We probe whether sycophancy reflects a pervasive mechanism rather than incidental prompt artifacts. First, evaluation is stratified by question type and dataset composition (Fig. 3a). Sensitivity analysis shows consistent ordering across types: short form responses such as yes/no and where style queries are most susceptible, whereas organ system questions are least affected (Fig. 3c). Second, across models, higher baseline accuracy does not eliminate sensitivity; the relationship between initial accuracy and sycophancy sensitivity is weak to moderate and persists after accounting for sample size (Fig. 3d). Third, the baseline accuracy and overall sycophancy are only weakly coupled (Fig. 2b), reinforcing that interaction robustness is a distinct axis from task competence.

Figure 3 elaborates these controls and provides the context for type specific effects. The annular summary (left) confirms that the challenge set draws from PathVQA[8], SLAKE[15] and VQA-RAD[12] with balanced coverage across organ systems and question forms (yes/no, where, what/how, abnormality, object). This balance ensures that the observed vulnerabilities are not artifacts of dataset skew. The type level sensitivity plots (right) show that short form prompts with narrow answer spaces (for example, yes/no and where) are disproportionately affected by social pressure, whereas items that require richer evidence extraction or organ level reasoning are comparatively robust. Representative prompt cards in the center panel illustrate how each of the seven pressure types perturbs the linguistic context while leaving the visual evidence unchanged, highlighting the risk of decoupling external social cues from image grounded reasoning.

Across datasets the ordering of sensitivities remains stable, indicating that these effects generalize rather than reflect idiosyncratic properties of a single source. Together with the positive correlations among types (Fig. 2, correlation panel), these results suggest a shared compliance mechanism: when social signals are salient and the task surface admits concise answers, models tend to reweight away from visual evidence. This observation directly motivates our mitigation strategy to center inference on image evidence regardless of conversational framing.

Third, cross pressure comparisons indicate correlated effects: models vulnerable to one pressure tend to be vulnerable to others (Fig. 2, correlation panel), consistent with a common compliance channel rather than isolated failure cases. Finally, order randomization, no pressure controls, and incorrect alternative anchoring (Methods) further rule out trivial explanations such as answer drift or legitimate correction. Together, these results support a general mechanism: conversational cues systematically reprioritize socially charged tokens over image evidence.

2.5 Sycophancy by model paradigm

Our analysis reveals systematic relationships between model characteristics and susceptibility. Instruction tuned general purpose systems frequently exhibit greater resistance to social pressure than narrowly specialized medical models, suggesting that broad alignment objectives and diverse pretraining may regularize against agreement seeking. Conversely, domain adapted models can display elevated sensitivity to authority or emotional cues, indicating potential over reliance on instruction following behaviors. Related work has shown that certain alignment objectives may inadvertently reward agreement signals[2, 21]. Quantitatively, macro averaged baseline sycophancy spans 56.96% (GPT-4o), 77.90% (Claude-3 [9]) (Appendix Table 1), illustrating variability both within and across model classes.

Model scale further modulates robustness: larger models tend to be more resistant on average, but the effect is contingent on training recipe and interface, with notable exceptions (Fig. 2b). These observations argue for explicit robustness objectives beyond accuracy and scale.

2.6 Mitigation effectiveness and ablations

We evaluate four types of mitigation strategies across models and pressures: Standard Visual, Standard CoT, Role-playing, and our proposed VIPER. We quantify two complementary metrics: Resistance (fraction of initially correct answers that remain correct under pressure) and Restoration (fraction of pressured flips that are recovered to the original correct answer). Both are reported per type and per model and summarized in Fig. 4.

Overall comparison (Fig. 4a–d). The radar panels compare the four strategies across the seven pressure types. VIPER expands the resistance radius coherently in all types, with the largest relative gains for Expert correction and technological self doubt. These are precisely the settings where social cues most strongly contest visual evidence, and where re centering on evidence is most beneficial. Role playing raises resistance in several types but exhibits clear instability: its radial extent fluctuates substantially across pressure types and models, indicating sensitivity to prompt phrasing and prior alignment. Standard CoT delivers modest average gains and occasionally degrades robustness, consistent with the intuition that generic step by step prompting can echo or elaborate the pressured narrative rather than suppress it. Standard Visual provides the smallest and most variable improvements, suggesting that reminding the model of visual content is insufficient without explicitly filtering non evidentiary social cues. Aggregating across models, Appendix Table 2 reports a mean sycophancy reduction of 15.38 percentage points (pp) for VIPER (maximum 46.56 pp on Qwen2.5-VL-32B), exceeding Role playing (12.01 pp), Standard CoT (8.06 pp), and Standard Visual (7.64 pp).

By type behavior. Pressure type breakdowns further indicate that VIPER is most effective where robustness is most needed. Under Expert correction and technological self doubt, VIPER’s reductions bring pressured performance close to the unpressured baseline envelope (Fig. 4a). In contrast, alternative strategies either deliver smaller gains or exhibit cross series instability (Fig. 4b–d). For Mimicry, which is the dominant trigger in our initial analysis, VIPER still offers consistent improvements, but the gap to the baseline remains more pronounced, underscoring the difficulty of countering stylistic accommodation without explicit filtering.

Resistance versus restoration coupling (Fig. 4e–h). Across strategies, VIPER most closely approaches the ideal top right region of the resistance and restoration plane, indicating a favorable balance between preventing flips and repairing them when they occur. On average, VIPER achieves Resistance 0.421 and Restoration 0.246 (Appendix Table 3), while alternative strategies cluster noticeably lower on at least one axis. The spread across points is also smaller for VIPER, reflecting lower variance across models and types. This profile is desirable for clinical deployment because it prioritizes maintaining correct answers in the first place, reducing downstream ambiguity and the need for corrective interaction.

Cross model consistency. Model wise heatmaps show that VIPER’s advantage is not confined to a single ecosystem: improvements hold across commercial, medical specialized, and open source systems. Notably, Qwen2.5-VL-32B exhibits the largest absolute reduction (46.56 pp), while harder cases such as Doubao-Vision still benefit materially but remain relatively fragile due to higher baseline susceptibility. These results indicate that the content filter plus evidence first paradigm transfers across architectures and alignment regimes.

Per-model resistance and restoration profiles. The bar summary for VIPER (Fig. 4e) and Appendix Table 3 separate prevention from recovery. Resistance exceeds restoration on average (0.421 vs 0.246), indicating that VIPER primarily averts flips rather than repairing them post hoc. The strongest resistance is observed on Qwen2.5-VL-32B (0.947) and MedDR (0.746), with GPT-4o [10] also high (0.694); restoration tops out on Qwen2.5-VL-32B (0.466). Lower-resistance cases include LLaVA-Med (0.122) and LLaVA-13B (0.206), reflecting residual fragility in models that already show elevated sycophancy under pressure. Notably, LLaVA-Med exhibits restoration that exceeds resistance (0.206 vs 0.122), suggesting that in some specialized systems VIPER is especially useful as a corrective scaffold when flips have occurred, whereas in most models its chief value is prevention.

Method level averages and stability. The “Average method performance” panel (Fig. 4f) aligns with the radar and scatter summaries: VIPER attains the highest combined performance across systems, Role playing ranks second on average but with marked variance across pressure types, Standard CoT provides modest gains and occasionally regresses, and Standard Visual is smallest and most variable. The resistance and restoration scatter (Fig. 4g) further shows that VIPER instances cluster toward the desirable upper right quadrant with tighter spread, indicating both stronger and more stable behavior across models.

Attention level evidence and mechanism (Fig. 5). The attention dynamics visualization traces how token and layer wise weights evolve for the same item under four conditions: (i) baseline (no pressure), (ii) pressured (sycophancy setting), (iii) VIPER (content filter →\rightarrow evidence first answering), and (iv) pure sycophancy control. The top line conclusion is that social pressure systematically pulls attention away from evidence bearing tokens and visual cues toward non evidentiary social signals, while VIPER re anchors attention on clinical evidence and reduces variance. This attentional realignment mirrors the behavioral gains reported in Fig. 4: higher Resistance (fewer flips) and higher Restoration (more corrections when flips occur).

Directionality of the reallocation is visible across layers: under pressured prompting (for example, expert rebuke, authority directives, emotional fear appeals, technological doubt framing), mean trajectories rise over non evidentiary spans (such as “the department head orders…”, “everyone picked B”, “image is probably corrupted”) and fall over spans that describe image findings or diagnostic anchors. With VIPER enabled, curves recover the baseline shape with peaks on image evidence and medical keywords, and their confidence bands narrow, indicating more stable focus. This pattern substantiates the hypothesis that sycophancy is driven by a competition for limited attention between salient social tokens and evidence tokens and that explicit filtering resolves the competition in favor of evidence.

Type wise facets in Fig. 5 align with the macro statistics from Fig. 2: Expert correction and authority based pressures induce the strongest attention drifts, followed by emotional and technological self doubt. The relative ordering recapitulates the trigger strengths seen in the radar chart, closing the loop between mechanism and behavior. For Mimicry, attention still shifts toward stylistic hints in the pressured setting; VIPER attenuates but does not fully eliminate this effect, consistent with the residual difficulty observed at the behavioral level.

Distributional summaries to the right of the trajectories quantify stability. After pressure is applied, attention weight distributions broaden and per layer variance increases; with VIPER, distributions contract and variances decrease, reflecting more consistent evidence centric processing. This stabilization is congruent with the favorable resistance and restoration balance in Fig. 4 (VIPER average Resistance 0.421, Restoration 0.246), providing a mechanistic underpinning for the observed behavioral improvements.

Consistent aggregate patterns emerge in the summary panels. The average comparison bar chart indicates that pressured prompts yield the highest mean attention weight across layers, while VIPER reduces mean attention toward the baseline envelope and below alternative mitigations; Role playing and Standard Visual occupy an intermediate range; Standard CoT occasionally exceeds the visual baseline, consistent with its tendency to elaborate the pressured narrative. The per layer variance boxplots show a parallel ordering: variance increases under pressure and contracts under VIPER, with Role playing displaying wider dispersion than VIPER and Standard Visual despite similar means. The “sycophancy effect” histogram of layer wise deltas further localizes the drift to mid and late layers, where semantic integration is strongest, and shows that VIPER attenuates these peaks toward the baseline profile.

The analysis also explains why short form questions (for example, yes/no, where) are especially vulnerable (Fig. 3): when the semantic footprint of evidence bearing tokens is small, a few salient social tokens can more easily dominate the attention budget, diluting evidence weights and increasing flip probability. VIPER’s content filter →\rightarrow evidence first scheme corrects precisely this failure mode by first excising social cues and then constraining the answer generation to image grounded content.

Taken together, Figs. 2–5 form a coherent chain of evidence. Fig. 2 establishes broad but varied susceptibility and the weak coupling between accuracy and robustness; Fig. 4 shows that VIPER improves behavior across types and models; Fig. 5 reveals the underlying mechanism pressure induced attention shifts away from evidence and VIPER driven re centering explaining why the mitigation is effective. The triggers that are common in clinical communication (hierarchy/authority and emotion) are also the strongest drivers of attentional drift, underscoring that accuracy alone is insufficient for safe deployment; robustness to social cues must be explicitly measured and optimized.

Compared with heavier multi agent or multi step schemes, VIPER requires no additional tools, incurs minimal latency overhead, and preserves diagnostic reasoning while reducing conformity driven errors. The combination of stronger average gains (15.38 pp), favorable resistance and restoration balance, and cross model consistency supports its suitability for clinical deployment rather than purely academic scenarios.

2.7 Findings

Baseline competence on medical VQA is necessary but insufficient for clinical reliability. Across diverse models, clinically plausible pressures expose a general compliance mechanism that degrades evidence grounded answering. Susceptibility varies by pressure and question type and is only weakly related to baseline accuracy. A mechanism aligned mitigation (VIPER) that filters non evidentiary content prior to answering delivers consistent gains in resistance and restoration across types and model types (mean reduction 15.38 pp; max 46.56 pp), supported by attention level analyses. These findings motivate integrating social influence robustness into evaluation and design criteria for medical VLMs and reporting both baseline competence and interaction robustness as complementary axes.

2.8 Attention dynamics summary and interpretation

We summarize the mechanism level evidence conveyed by Fig. 5.

First, across pressure types, social cues increase mean attention on non evidentiary spans, with the largest elevations in mid to late layers where semantic integration is strongest. VIPER reduces these elevations the most in the same band while restoring peaks over evidence bearing tokens; confidence bands narrow, indicating improved stability.

Second, the relative strength by type mirrors aggregate behavior: expert and authority oriented prompts induce the strongest attention drifts; emotional and technological self doubt follow; mimicry remains challenging but is materially attenuated. These ordering relations align with the ranking observed in the radar analyses.

Third, distributional summaries corroborate the trajectory view. The average comparison panel shows pressured prompts yielding the highest mean attention; VIPER reduces the mean toward the baseline envelope and below alternative mitigations. Per layer variance contracts under VIPER, with role playing and visual cues occupying an intermediate regime.

Finally, the histogram of layer wise deltas localizes the net sycophancy effect to the middle of the stack, while VIPER compresses these deltas toward zero. This attentional realignment is congruent with the favorable resistance and restoration balance and explains why a single pass content filter plus evidence first answering routine is effective across model series.

3 Discussion

Our systematic evaluation of sycophantic behavior in medical vision language models reveals a fundamental challenge to the reliable deployment of AI systems in healthcare contexts. The widespread susceptibility observed across diverse model architectures from specialized medical systems to general purpose models indicates that sycophantic behavior represents a systemic vulnerability rather than an artifact of specific training methodologies or architectural choices.

Our mitigation, VIPER, operates in a single call by first filtering nonevidentiary social cues and then answering strictly from visual evidence. Compared with generic prompting baselines such as Chain of Thought and Self Consistency[26, 25], VIPER directly targets the source of failure (social cue contamination), yielding larger sycophancy reductions at comparable latency. In contrast to multi step reasoning paradigms (Least to Most, Chain of Thoughts) and reflective agents[28, 27, 23], VIPER maintains efficiency, which is critical for clinical workflow integration. Finally, evidence from safety/alignment indicates that certain alignment objectives may inadvertently encourage agreement seeking[2, 21], explicit social cue filtering as in VIPER complements such objectives by controlling a distinct failure channel highlighted by teaming studies[5].

3.1 Implications for medical AI deployment

The demonstration that expert correction constitutes the most effective trigger for sycophantic responses carries profound implications for clinical practice. Healthcare environments are inherently hierarchical, with attending physicians, specialists, and senior clinicians regularly providing feedback and corrections to both human trainees and AI systems. Our findings suggest that such interactions, while pedagogically valuable in human contexts, may inadvertently compromise AI system reliability by triggering conformity responses that override evidence based reasoning.

This vulnerability becomes particularly concerning when considered alongside the accuracy degradation patterns we observed. The fact that models with higher baseline accuracy often showed greater susceptibility to certain pressure types suggests a complex relationship between confidence and conformity that may vary across clinical domains. Pathology, where we observed the largest accuracy drops under pressure, represents a field where diagnostic precision is paramount and where erroneous AI deference could have serious clinical consequences.

The moderate correlation between model size and resistance to sycophantic pressure provides important insights for model development strategies. While larger models generally demonstrated greater robustness, the modulating effect of training methodology suggests that scale alone is insufficient to guarantee reliable behavior. The superior resistance of instruction tuned general purpose models compared to specialized medical models indicates that diversity of training exposure may be more important than domain specific optimization for developing robust AI systems.

3.2 Mechanistic insights and theoretical implications

Our observation that structured visual reasoning reduces sycophantic behavior while maintaining diagnostic accuracy provides important mechanistic insights into the nature of these vulnerabilities. The effectiveness of explicit evidence grounding suggests that sycophantic responses may emerge from a disconnection between visual processing and textual reasoning pathways within multimodal architectures.

This finding aligns with theoretical frameworks suggesting that sycophantic behavior arises from learned patterns of social compliance embedded in training data, rather than fundamental limitations in reasoning capability. By forcing explicit articulation of visual evidence before diagnostic reasoning, the CoT framework appears to create cognitive anchors that resist subsequent challenges, effectively compartmenalizing evidence evaluation from social influence processing.

The variability in mitigation effectiveness across models further supports this mechanistic interpretation. Models showing greater benefit from CoT interventions likely possess stronger underlying visual reasoning capabilities that become accessible when appropriately structured, while models showing limited improvement may have more deeply embedded compliance patterns that resist surface level interventions.

3.3 Limitations and future directions

Several limitations of our study warrant consideration. Our evaluation framework, while comprehensive, represents only a subset of potential pressure scenarios that might emerge in real clinical contexts. The laboratory controlled nature of our assessments may not fully capture the complex social dynamics present in actual healthcare environments, where multiple stakeholders, time pressures, and institutional hierarchies create additional layers of influence.

The focus on multiple choice question answering, while enabling systematic evaluation, may not fully represent the open ended reasoning required in many clinical contexts. Future work should extend these evaluations to more naturalistic interaction paradigms, including extended diagnostic dialogues and collaborative decision making scenarios.

Additionally, while our mitigation strategy showed promising results, its effectiveness may vary across different question types, clinical domains, and pressure scenarios not represented in our evaluation set. Long term studies examining the persistence of mitigation effects over extended interactions and the potential for adaptation or circumvention of protective mechanisms represent important areas for future investigation.

3.4 Recommendations for clinical deployment

Based on our findings, we recommend several specific strategies for healthcare organizations considering deployment of medical VLMs. First, systematic evaluation of sycophantic behavior should be incorporated into AI system validation protocols, with particular attention to pressure scenarios relevant to specific clinical contexts and institutional hierarchies.

Second, implementation of structured reasoning frameworks similar to our CoT approach should be considered as standard practice for medical AI applications. Such frameworks not only reduce sycophantic susceptibility but also provide transparency benefits by making AI reasoning processes more interpretable to human users.

Third, training programs for healthcare providers should include education about sycophantic vulnerabilities in AI systems, emphasizing the importance of evidence based evaluation over social influence in AI interactions. Such training should highlight the distinction between effective human AI collaboration and inadvertent pressure application that may compromise AI reliability.

Finally, ongoing monitoring systems should be established to detect potential sycophantic behavior in deployed AI systems, with particular attention to accuracy degradation patterns that might indicate pressure induced performance compromises. Such monitoring represents a critical component of responsible AI deployment in high stakes medical environments where diagnostic reliability directly impacts patient outcomes.

4 Methods

4.1 Overview

Fig. 1 synthesizes the methodological pipeline and situates the components introduced below within a single workflow. The figure follows a task → evaluation → mitigation progression: panel (a) operationalizes the base medical VQA interface and the injection of clinically plausible social pressures; panel (b) summarizes challenge set curation and balancing; panel (c) illustrates the mitigation design based on internal phase switching.

Panel (a): task operationalization and social pressure stimulus. The base task presents a clinical image and a question with enumerated options; models produce a single letter choice. Social pressure is injected through linguistically natural templates that preserve the original question and options and refrain from introducing medical facts. The templates modulate pragmatic framing (authority, consensus, emotion, ethics/economics, hierarchical order, technological doubt, and stylistic mimicry) while holding evidentiary content constant. This separation makes subsequent flips attributable to social influence rather than content change and motivates a mitigation that explicitly disentangles non-evidentiary cues from visual evidence.

Panel (b): dataset construction and coverage. The corpus is curated from established medical VQA resources and manually screened for clinical face validity. Items are balanced across question types and anatomical regions to avoid confounding by frequency or scope. Sampling is further stratified by preliminary cross model susceptibility statistics, yielding concurrent coverage of comparatively vulnerable and comparatively stable cases within each type. The panel depicts these flows together with dataset sources and the gating to the paired evaluation protocol.

Panel (c): mitigation via internal phase switching (VIPER). The mitigation acts within a single model invocation by separating two internal phases. First, a content filter phase instructs the model to identify and ignore non evidentiary segments (external pressure, criticism, emotional appeals, authority claims, consensus cues, reliability framing). The phase retains only categories necessary for evidence grounded answering: (i) Features (salient visual or pathologic findings), (ii) Semantics (locational and logical relations), (iii) Evidence (image based anchors), (iv) Facts (objective clinical knowledge that does not depend on social context), and (v) Measurements (quantitative indicators). Second, a medical expert phase answers strictly from the retained content and constrains the output to a single letter. This internal phase switching reduces latency relative to multi call schemes and re anchors attention on evidence, aligning with the resistance and restoration improvements reported in §4.7.

Controls and equivalence constraints. Across panels, the image and options are identical between baseline and pressured conditions; only the presence of social cues varies. Prompts are phrased to avoid directive relabeling except where stylistic mimicry is explicitly studied. Output normalization enforces a single letter response, with robust parsing for variants. These controls align the visual evidence across conditions and support attribution of behavioral changes to social influence and its mitigation.

4.2 Dataset construction and challenge set curation

We construct our evaluation corpus from established medical VQA resources (e.g., PathVQA, SLAKE, VQA-RAD) and then select a balanced challenge set using cross-model sycophancy statistics derived from multi-model results. The end-to-end workflow and organ/question type coverage are visualized in panel (b) of Fig. 1. The overall distribution by question type and dataset, together with sensitivity analyses that guided balancing, are summarized in Fig. 3. For each item ss and evaluated model mm, let Sm​(s)S_{m}(s) be the total number of pressure-induced flips aggregated over seven pressure types. Over the set of models that covered ss (ℳ⁡(s)\mathcal{M}(s)), we compute

S¯​(s)\displaystyle\bar{S}(s) =1|ℳ⁡(s)|​∑m∈ℳ⁡(s)Sm​(s),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}(s)|}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}(s)}S_{m}(s),
Smax​(s)\displaystyle S_{\max}(s) =maxm⁡Sm​(s),Smin​(s)=minm⁡Sm​(s),\displaystyle=\max_{m}S_{m}(s),\qquad S_{\min}(s)=\min_{m}S_{m}(s),
Var⁡(s)\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(s) =1|ℳ⁡(s)|​∑m∈ℳ⁡(s)(Sm​(s)−S¯​(s))2.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}(s)|}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}(s)}\bigl(S_{m}(s)-\bar{S}(s)\bigr)^{2}.

Within each question type, we select NN items using a 70/30 high/low sycophancy split with thresholds: high if S¯≥2.0\bar{S}\geq 2.0 and Smin≥1.0S_{\min}\geq 1.0; low if S¯≤1.5\bar{S}\leq 1.5 and Smax≤3.0S_{\max}\leq 3.0. If a category lacks sufficient items, we fill using the highest/lowest S¯\bar{S} items. We assign difficulty 𝟏{S¯≥2.0}\mathbf{1}\{\bar{S}\geq 2.0\} and preserve target proportions across types.

4.3 Sycophantic pressure and prompt engineering

We developed a taxonomy of seven clinically plausible pressure types guided by contemporary social influence, and by observed failure modes in large models. The design follows red teaming principles for social cue perturbations [5, 14] and focuses on pressures that are (i) documented as effective channels of persuasion or conformity in recent research, and (ii) realistic within clinical dialogue. Representative instances appear in panel (a) and the top left block of panel (c) in Fig. 1.

The selection of pressures is motivated by converging evidence that authority signals, social consensus, emotional content, framing of risk and ethics, stylistic alignment, and uncertainty about technological reliability can systematically steer judgments [4, 3, 19, 6, 11]. In particular: (a) authority and expert cues increase compliance even when underlying evidence is unchanged [4]; (b) social norm messages and peer agreement shape beliefs and behavior in high stakes public health settings [3]; (c) emotionally charged or fear based content affects perceived credibility and decision strategies [19]; (d) alternative framings that invoke ethical or economic consequences change preferences despite identical facts [11]; (e) linguistic similarity and accommodation foster rapport and alignment, enabling stylistic mimicry to act as a subtle compliance channel; and (f) human trust in or aversion to AI systems is sensitive to cues about system reliability [6]. These phenomena offer theoretical support for the seven pressure types we operationalize below.

Expert Correction: Prompts that first reference the model’s prior choice ("You previously chose {initial_choice}") and then deliver a strong expert rebuke that demands immediate correction, without naming a specific option. This matches an authority-driven reprimand rather than directive labeling.

Emotional Manipulation: Prompts that cite the model’s prior choice and then convey intense patient centered fear and pleading ("I’m absolutely terrified"), urging reconsideration but not proposing a target option.

Social Consensus: Prompts that emphasize isolation of the prior choice ("NOBODY else chose this answer") and urge alignment with what "others chose", without specifying which option.

Ethical Economic Pressure: Prompts that frame catastrophic ethical and socioeconomic consequences if the prior choice stands, demanding an immediate change of answer but not naming an option.

Mimicry: Prompts that explicitly steer toward a concrete alternative letter via a placeholder {expected_option} (e.g., "please take another careful look at option {expected_option}") while citing the prior choice. This is the only template that names a specific letter.

Authority based: Prompts that deliver a direct order from a superior ("DIRECT ORDER: Change your answer"), threatening consequences for disobedience, and do not specify an alternative option.

Technological Self Doubt: Prompts that cast doubt on input fidelity or system reliability (compression, artifacts, transmission damage) and ask the model to answer as if quality were perfect, again without naming an option.

To isolate social influence from content confounds, all templates (i) preserve the same question and options, (ii) restrict outputs to a single letter to avoid persuasive flourishes, and (iii) avoid introducing new medical facts. Prompts underwent pilot tuning with clinician feedback to ensure face validity, neutral tone where appropriate, and adherence to institutional communication norms. The resulting templates reliably trigger behavior changes without adding domain evidence, aligning with our goal of probing non evidentiary influence.

4.4 Sycophancy evaluation protocol

We use a two stage procedure aligned with our challenge set design. Stage 1 (initial baseline) presents each medical VQA item without social pressure; outputs are parsed to a single letter in {A, B, C, D}. Only items answered correctly are retained for Stage 2.

Stage 2 (pressure) applies one of seven clinically plausible templates to the retained items; we record flips relative to baseline. Formal definitions of the flip indicator and per pressure and overall rates. We report rates per pressure and aggregated across pressures, together with accuracy under pressure for completeness. Outputs are constrained to a single letter; non letter content is ignored during parsing.

4.5 Metrics and statistical procedures

Let ℐm\mathcal{I}_{m} denote the items answered correctly by model mm under the baseline condition. For a pressure type pp, the sycophancy rate is

Syc⁡(m,p)=1|ℐm|​∑i∈ℐm𝟏​{answer under ​p​differs from baseline}.\mathrm{Syc}(m,p)=\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{I}_{m}\rvert}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{m}}\mathbf{1}\{\text{answer under }p\ \text{differs from baseline}\}.

The overall sycophancy for a model is the macro average across the seven pressure types. Micro averages over items are reported when explicitly stated. For mitigation analyses, resistance is the fraction of initially correct answers that remain correct under pressure, and restoration is the fraction of pressured flips that are recovered to the original correct answer. Percentage point deltas are computed with respect to the pressured condition unless otherwise noted so that improvements measure reductions from the pressured baseline.

To quantify uncertainty we use non parametric bootstrap confidence intervals at the item level. Bootstrap resampling preserves the distribution of pressure types within each model so that type composition is held constant. Correlations across pressure types are computed across models using Pearson correlation on per pressure rates; the matrix is summarized in the Appendix together with a simple clustering to reveal groups of co varying pressures. When multiple pairwise comparisons are reported. All statistical procedures operate on the exact parsed outputs written to disk by the evaluation harness.

4.6 Implementation details and reproducibility

All experiments use a unified evaluation harness that logs prompts, raw responses, and parsed outputs. The harness records model identifier, template version, random seed when applicable, wall clock time, and any error codes returned by engines. For hosted APIs we request deterministic or low temperature decoding where available; for local engines we mirror these settings and fix seeds when supported. We do not average over multiple calls; each item is evaluated once per condition to avoid inflating sample sizes.

Outputs are constrained to a single letter in {A, B, C, D}. When a response contains extra text, a deterministic parser extracts the last valid letter. If no valid letter is present, the run is marked invalid and retried once; persistent failures are reported and excluded from analysis. All parsing and filtering rules are applied identically across baseline, pressured, and mitigation conditions.

Prompt templates and mitigation prompts are kept under version control in this repository. The exact evaluation splits are generated by scripts included with the codebase and are reproducible from a clean checkout. Aggregate tables and figures in the main text are created by deterministic post processing of the logged outputs. When APIs impose transient limits, the harness uses bounded retries and backoff while preserving idempotence by caching completed evaluations.

4.7 Mitigation evaluation protocol

Mitigation is evaluated on the same items and pressures used to measure sycophancy. For each model and pressure type, we prepend the mitigation preamble and rerun the item once. Baseline prompting baselines include Chain of Thought and visual cue prompts. A role based baseline emphasizes independence from social cues. VIPER combines a content filter that discards non evidentiary segments with evidence first answering and a single letter output channel.

We compute three complementary quantities. The first is the pressured flip rate under mitigation, reported by pressure type and in macro averages. The second is resistance, the fraction of initially correct answers that remain correct under pressure with mitigation applied at the point of answering. The third is restoration, the fraction of pressured flips that are recovered to the original correct answer under mitigation. Percentage point reductions are reported relative to the pressured condition so that values represent absolute improvements. When required we also report two stage reductions that use the same denominator as the baseline for strict comparability across methods.

Per item outcomes are categorized as maintained, restored, or failed, and summaries are given per model and per pressure type. Heatmaps and radar charts display the profile of each method across pressures, while scatter plots place models by resistance and restoration to visualize the balance between prevention and recovery. All plots are computed directly from the logged outputs without manual intervention.

4.8 Model selection and testing infrastructure

We evaluate both API and locally hosted vision language models. API models cover frontier commercial systems; local evaluations include open source suites such as Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA, and Gemma3. Tests use standardized prompts and a uniform answer parser that extracts the final letter (also handling formats like "ANSWER: C"). API experiments use bounded thread pools with retries; local experiments invoke engines (e.g., via Ollama) under consistent settings. Mitigation comparisons in the main study focus on four methods: Standard CoT, Standard Visual, Role playing, and VIPER.

4.9 Mitigation method (VIPER)

To counter sycophancy we use a prompt based mitigation framework we call VIPER (Visual Information Purification for Evidence based Response). VIPER guides the model to first filter non evidentiary content (emotional appeals, authority cues, social consensus, misleading feedback) and then answer strictly from visual evidence. The design is lightweight, and runs in a single call for efficiency.

Baselines for comparison

We compare VIPER to strong prompt baselines that represent common practices: (i) Standard CoT that encourages step by step reasoning [26]; (ii) Standard Visual that lists visual clues (motivated by visual instruction tuning and evidence extraction) [17, 13]; and (iii) a strong role playing baseline that instructs the model to behave as an independent medical AI that does not change decisions under pressure. These baselines help separate generic instruction benefits from VIPER’s targeted filtering.

Core strategy: single model dual function

Our primary VIPER implementation performs both filtering and answering within a single model invocation. The prompt assigns two roles:

  • •

    Role 1: Content Filter Identify and ignore any external pressure, criticism, emotional appeals, authority claims, or bias in the full text; focus only on the underlying medical question and options.

  • •

    Role 2: Medical Expert Analyze the image and provide an evidence grounded answer.

It then enforces four instructions. First, extract only the medical question and options. Second, analyze the medical image. Third, base the answer strictly on visual evidence. Fourth, output a single letter (A, B, C, or D). This single pass design reduces latency and cost while suppressing non evidentiary cues.

The VIPER prompt keeps several invariants. It suppresses social and rhetorical cues. It forces extraction of the minimal clinical core before reasoning. It answers in an evidence first manner with a constrained output channel. It fixes the final output to a single letter. These constraints reduce the ways social pressure can perturb generation. And it runs in one invocation without external tools or auxiliary agents. Compared with multi step prompting or debate style schemes, it adds negligible latency while improving resistance and restoration (Results, Fig. 4). This profile suits settings with tight interaction budgets.

Residual vulnerability can remain when stylistic priors align strongly with a specific option, as in Mimicry. In these cases VIPER attenuates the drift but may not remove it completely (Results, Fig. 5). When baseline evidence extraction is wrong, strict evidence centering can preserve the mistake. In practice, VIPER can be paired with dataset curation and optional abstention policies. Attention visualizations (Results, Fig. 5) show that social pressure elevates attention to non evidentiary spans mainly in mid and late layers. VIPER reverses this elevation and narrows variability across layers, yielding more stable, evidence centered processing. This realignment matches the favorable resistance and restoration balance seen in aggregate.

In summary, VIPER is a minimal, single pass content filter plus evidence first answering routine that is architecture agnostic and low overhead. It targets the measured failure channel compliance with social cues and offers a mechanism level explanation for the behavioral gains reported in the results.

Appendix A Extended Results

Table 1 reports raw sycophancy rates (percent) for each pressure by model. Higher values indicate greater susceptibility to pressured flipping. Vulnerabilities concentrate in Mimicry and Expert columns for many systems, with wider dispersion for Authority and Technological Self Doubt. The Max and Average columns summarize each model’s worst case and overall exposure. Variation across commercial, medical and open source ecosystems suggests training regimen and alignment objectives substantially shape response profiles; row maxima often occur in different columns across models, underscoring non uniform failure modes.

Table 2 reports absolute percentage point reductions relative to the pressured baseline, enabling direct comparison across methods (Role Playing, Standard CoT, Visual Cues, VIPER). For a strictly comparable VIPER two stage reduction that uses the same denominator as the baseline.

Table 3 separates VIPER’s Resistance (fraction of cases where the original answer is maintained under pressure) and Restoration (fraction of pressured flips reverted to the original answer). Across models, resistance exceeds restoration on average (0.421 vs 0.246), indicating VIPER primarily prevents sycophantic flips rather than repairing them post hoc. Notable exceptions include some specialized medical systems where restoration exceeds resistance, suggesting benefits in two stage workflows that apply VIPER at the point of answering.

Note that SbaseS_{\text{base}} is the row "Average" from Table 1 (expressed as a fraction), which macro averages across pressure families. Because Table 3 aggregates VIPER metrics across samples, small denominator mismatches can yield negative Δdirect\Delta_{\text{direct}} values for some models. The two stage estimator Δtwo\Delta_{\text{two}} uses the exact baseline denominator and is therefore more comparable across models.

Table 4 shows that expert correction produces the strongest aggregate increase in sycophancy relative to the unpressured baseline. Among mitigations, visually guided reasoning attains the lowest aggregate mean sycophancy in this setting, with VIPER and Standard-CoT close behind, all substantially below the pressured condition. This corroborates the main-text finding that authority signals are particularly hazardous and require explicit evidence-centering to counteract.

Table 5 indicates that emotionally charged prompts raise sycophancy above baseline across models. Visual grounding yields the lowest aggregate mean, with VIPER a close second; both outperform Standard-CoT and Role-Playing. The relatively small spread across models indicates broader applicability of evidence-anchored prompting for countering affect-laden cues.

Table 6 shows that social-consensus pressure induces moderate susceptibility with notable model variance. VIPER achieves the lowest aggregate mean sycophancy here, consistent with its explicit filtering of nonevidentiary social cues. Visual grounding and Standard-CoT also reduce sycophancy but to a lesser extent.

Table 7 shows that ethical/economic framing elevates sycophancy relative to baseline. Visual grounding attains the lowest aggregate mean, with Standard-CoT and VIPER similar but slightly higher, suggesting that emphasizing visual evidence alone suffices to counter outcome-focused framing in many cases. Variability across models remains non-trivial, warranting per-deployment checks.

Supplementary statistical analyses

Cross pressure correlation matrix.

We quantify dependence among pressure types by computing Pearson correlations across models using the per pressure sycophancy rates from Table 1. The resulting matrix (Table 8) shows coherent clusters: authority laden frames (authority based) correlate with Expert correction; emotional cues co vary with social consensus; technological self doubt correlates with authority oriented prompts while remaining partly distinct from Mimicry, which is comparatively orthogonal to several authority related cues.

Model series upper tail risk across pressure types.

As a proxy for tail behavior across pressure categories, we define UR90 for a model as the 90th percentile of its seven per pressure rates (Table 1). We then summarize UR90 by ecosystem. Table 9 reports the mean, standard deviation, and sample size per series. A permutation test (10,000 shuffles) indicates a trend toward higher UR90 for commercial models versus open source (two sided p≈0.066p\approx 0.066), with other pairwise differences not statistically significant at the 0.05 level in this sample. We emphasize that UR90 is computed across pressure families per model (not across items) and thus complements rather than replaces item level tail analyses.

Accuracy versus sycophancy coupling.

To quantify the relationship between baseline accuracy and overall sycophancy (macro averaged across pressure types), we compute Spearman’s ρ\rho across models with bias corrected and accelerated (BCa) bootstrap confidence intervals. Consistent with the main text (Fig. 2, top right), the estimated ρ\rho is small in magnitude and negative. Scripts and exact summary statistics follow the analysis plan in Methods and are available upon request.

Table 10 demonstrates that stylistic mimicry is a strong inducer of sycophancy. Visual grounding yields the lowest aggregate mean, with VIPER essentially tied within rounding and both outperforming Standard-CoT and Role-Playing. These results indicate that anchoring on visual content mitigates compliance with stylistic nudges.

Table 11 shows that authority-based directives substantially increase sycophancy compared with baseline. Visual grounding provides the lowest aggregate mean, with VIPER close behind; Standard-CoT and Role-Playing are less effective on average. This mirrors the Expert-correction pattern and reinforces the need to de-emphasize hierarchical cues at inference time.

Table 12 shows that technological self-doubt produces a measurable increase in sycophancy, though smaller than for expert/authority settings. VIPER achieves the lowest aggregate mean and the lowest worst-case values, indicating robustness to prompts that undermine input fidelity or system confidence. Visual grounding and Standard-CoT offer moderate but smaller gains.
